item.title: Binding dissimilar biomaterials
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01962-0

Biopolymer composites offer a sustainable route to multifunctional materials, but integrating chemically distinct biopolymers remains challenging owing to mismatched interfacial interactions. Now, researchers report a small molecule strategy that modulates biomass networks, improving their structural integration and functionality.
item.dc:title: Binding dissimilar biomaterials
item.dc:creator: Chunhua Wang
Wei Lin

item.title: Material circularity implications of battery degradation in shared electric mobility
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01969-7

Shared mobility aims to save materials, yet intensive use accelerates battery degradation and may alter these savings. This study assesses the implications of shared mobility by coupling fleet projections, battery degradation and dynamic material flow analysis in China.
item.dc:title: Material circularity implications of battery degradation in shared electric mobility

Guochang Xu
Wu Chen

item.title: Artificial intelligence for life-cycle-aware sustainable materials discovery
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01950-4

Materials discovery by artificial intelligence rarely considers scalability, environmental impacts or end-of-life management, prioritizing functional performance. This Perspective suggests a roadmap for embedding life-cycle considerations in the discovery process to design sustainable materials from the start.

item.title: Small-molecule-bound biopolymer networks for sustainable multifunctional composites
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01967-9

Combining biomaterials of different nature can yield sustainable composites with otherwise inaccessible properties. This study presents a strategy to overcome interfacial mismatch between individual components, enabling efficient structural integration within mechanically strong, multifunctional films.

item.title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01971-z

Climate action reshapes who gains and loses from energy and environmental resources, raising new geopolitical questions. A study now quantifies four climate-related asset types across 169 countries and reveals uneven asset redistribution, with major powers often less affected.
item.dc:title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation

item.title: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01939-z

Deforestation-reducing development pathways may cut emissions, but it is unclear how workers can adapt given skill and geographic mobility constraints. Modelling job transitions in Brazil reveals that greener pathways benefit workers in high-skill occupations but increase low-skill unemployment, mitigated by mobility policies.
item.dc:title: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil

item.title: Assessing green-growth and degrowth pathways through institutional regime feasibility
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01951-3

Choosing a feasible economic growth trajectory to mitigate climate change cannot hinge on only gross domestic product trends. This Perspective presents a framework to understand where each possible growth path places its heaviest burdens and shows that such understanding is critical to inform policy decisions.
item.dc:title: Assessing green-growth and degrowth pathways through institutional regime feasibility
item.dc:creator: Ingo Pies
Felix Carl Schultz
